senses: Any of several large, arboreal Old World monkeys in the genera Cercocebus and Lophocebus.
ety: So called by Buffon from Mangaby, in Madagascar, where he erroneously supposed them to be native.

senses: Of a projection used in maps, architecture etc., in which the rays are parallel.
ety: From ortho- + -graph + -ic. Compare French orthographique, Latin orthographus, Ancient Greek ὀρθογράφος (orthográphos).

senses: A small chewy candy made with corn syrup, gelatin, and flavouring.
A lively Andalusian dance.
The clapping that accompanies it.
Synonym of hoggish (“resembling a pig”).
examples: Then the packing-houses in making lard got to dumping into the pans everything — heads, feet, etc. — and made a product which was offensive, having, as witness said, a "hoggy taste."

senses: Using the power of the military.
Related to the use of the military.
Tuna in solid (unflaked) form, packed in olive oil.
ety: From Italian tonno. Doublet of tuna.

senses: An ancient Greek stringed instrument, which could be considered a forerunner of the guitar.
ety: From Latin cithara, from Ancient Greek κιθάρα (kithára). Doublet of cither, guitar, kithara, kissar, and zither.

senses: Having an abnormally small head.
ety: From French microcéphalique, from Ancient Greek μικρός (mikrós, “small”) + κεφαλή (kephalḗ, “head”).

senses: A framework upon which laundry is aired; a clotheshorse.
One who chats or talks to excess.
Synonym of cootie catcher (“children's fortune-telling device”).
The orchid Epipactis gigantea.
A genre of light classical north Indian music.
An individual piece of music in this style.
examples: Subhra Guha's "rendition of the thumri is notable for its rich technique and aesthetic appeal emanating from her immaculate use of bol."
These courtesans sang beautiful tappas and thumris much to the delight of the citizens.

senses: The orange roughy, Hoplostethus atlanticus.
The front side of a flat object which is to be examined visually, as for reading, such as a sheet, leaf, coin or medal.
The right-hand page of a book of a script which reads from left to right, usually having an odd page number.
ety: Borrowed from Latin rēctō foliō (“on the right leaf, on the right page”), the ablative case of the Latin rēctus (“right”). Compare versus (“turned”).

senses: Any periodic sound, especially one composed of a fundamental and harmonics, as opposed to simple periodic sounds (sine tones).
A measure of the extent to which something is deformable (under standard conditions)
The character of being personal.
A doctrine of subjective idealism that regards personality as the means of interpreting reality.
A foot of this kind.
A decorative foot on a bathtub etc. resembling a claw.
A musician who programs or plays a synthesizer.
A person who treats diseases by means of medicinal herbs.
A temporary dwelling or booth used by practising Jews during Tabernacles (Sukkot).
Prepared with tomatoes, or in a tomato sauce.
Of pasta: In a seafood sauce. Of pizza: With seafood topping.
Having a grassy, herbaceous taste.
ety: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin vegetālis, from Latin vegetō.

senses: Any of many tropical fish, of the family Cichlidae, popular as aquarium fish.
A major change in appearance or form; a metamorphosis.
A change that exalts or glorifies.
superposition of one or more ideal-elements in comparison with other real ones, often through imagination but sometimes at the risk of confusing when not clearly realized.
ety: From Middle English transfiguracioun, from Old French transfiguracion, Anglo-Norman transfiguraciun, and Latin transfigūrātio.

senses: The ball used in that game.
ety: From (onomatopoeia) whiff (“to strike, to strikeout”) + ball. Not derived from whiffle, though both derive from same onomatopoeic sources, namely a sound of wind.

senses: Any material that forms a colloid (especially a gel) when mixed with water.
Any of a broad subclass of such materials that are of biologic origin or importance, most being biopolymers such as polysaccharides or proteins.
Such a material, made from agar, used to make dental impressions.
One who, or that which, smudges.
examples: Servile smudgers of history, prattling about an Emil Ludwig and a Thomas Mann season — meaning the Weimar period — as if it had produced me and as if I had used the Republic for a background!
The tools can get rather exotic - spinners, rubber stamps, airbrush, smudgers, and so on.

senses: To assist (someone or something) by granting a subsidy.
Something which is unpredictable.
Extreme strictness regarding moral scruples.
ety: Borrowed from French puritanisme, equivalent to puritan + -ism.

senses: One who practices agriculture, a farmer, a gardener.
An expert in agriculture who advises farmers.
In parts of South Asia, a gathering where poetry or classical music is performed for a small audience in an intimate setting.
ety: From Urdu محفل (mahfil), from Arabic مَحْفِل (maḥfil, “festive gathering to entertain or praise someone”).
examples: One of the most interesting descriptions in the Muraqqa’ is of the famous mehfils, the literary or musical evenings for which the city was then renowned.
The entire mehfil was babbling away but Bahadur's tense silence rang like an alarm in my head.

senses: An embankment to prevent inundation; as, the levees along the Mississippi.
The border of an irrigated field.
ety: From French levée, from lever (“to raise, rise”).

senses: The act or process of mutualizing.
Having, or growing in bunches.
ety: From Middle English bunchy, bonchy, equivalent to bunch + -y.

senses: A unit of length defined as exactly sixty-seven inches (approximately 1.70 meters).
ety: Derives from the height of Oliver R. Smoot, who had lain on the Harvard Bridge to measure it as a fraternity prank at MIT.

senses: A bandicoot rat; any of the genera Bandicota and Nesokia of rat-like rodents of southeast Asia.
ety: Ultimately from Telugu పందికొక్కు (pandikokku), from పంది (pandi, “pig, boar”) + కొక్కు (kokku, “bandicoot”); first used of Asian murids, now called bandicoot rats, thence applied to the Australian marsupials which bear some resemblance.

senses: A specialist in the leather processing industry, who dresses the leather by beating, rubbing, scraping and colouring.
One who grooms a horse with a curry comb.
ety: From Old French corier, from Latin coriarius (“tanner, currier”).

senses: A colony of breeding birds or other animals.
A crowded tenement.
examples: It was a rookery which had never been raided by the hunters, and in consequence the seals were mild-tempered and at the same time unafraid.

In winter rooks roost together in large numbers, and the roost may or may not be a rookery, but almost daily the local residents pay visits to the nesting trees, and about this time often begin playing at nest-building.
There are six rookeries either side of Haddiscoe Island, which average 283 nests each.
